claims.claim: At the Persian court the princes of the three nations begged him to accept the king's religion for a time and in appearance; he refused, crying "Loin de moi cette pensée de mentir jamais à mon Créateur, soit en apparence, soit réellement"
claims.witness: Lazar of Pharp, tr. Ghesarian (langlois t2 l.38817-38890)

claims.claim: The princes swore on the Gospel; he wept and consented to yield for a time, in appearance, to save the three nations; some of the princes seemed to bow in the fire temple
Some of the princes, on a royal councillor's advice, sent word they would conform to the king's belief
Lazar places himself at the end of the fifth century or the start of the sixth
claims.witness: Ghesarian's introduction to Lazar (langlois t2 l.35066-35069); a translator's date

claims.claim: General of the Armenians and lord of the Mamikonians, taught the Scriptures by the patriarch Sahak, his grandfather
claims.witness: Lazar of Pharp (langlois t2 l.38864-38865, 38943-38945; OCR 'son meul', read as 'son aïeul'); Neumann's preface (l.575-576), 'a grandson of Sahag the Great'

claims.claim: The people drove off the Mogbed and the Magi who tried to break open a church
Vasak, prince of Siunik, went over to the Persians
claims.witness: Elishe (l.3138-3139, 3287); Lazar of Pharp (langlois t2 l.39313, 41270-41280)

claims.claim: In 451 the armies met near the village of Avarayr on the plain of the Deghmut
claims.witness: Lazar of Pharp (langlois t2 l.40208-40209); Elishe, river Dekhmud (l.4105)

claims.claim: Speech before the battle: "Should the object of our lives be completed by a holy death in battle, let us meet it with a joyful heart"
claims.witness: Elishe (l.3910-3911); a speech as Elishe writes it

claims.claim: Scattered the Persian right wing with the elephants, then was "found worthy of martyrdom on the spot"
One thousand and thirty-six Armenians fell
claims.witness: Elishe (l.4221-4227); Lazar of Pharp (langlois t2 l.40458-40466, rough OCR); Ormanian, Vardan, eight generals and 1,027 men (l.2261-2262)

claims.claim: King Yazdegerd grieved on hearing of the death of the brave Vartan
He promised the Persian court a deed whose fame would ring out for ever; God took the promise and gave him the title of martyr, to last among all nations
Commemorated on Shrove-Thursday; listed among the saints with his 1,035 companions

contested_claims.sides: Ormanian: 26 May 451 (l.2256, 2452). Neumann's margin: June 2 (l.4147), and his preface, June 451 (l.758). The note in the French edition of Lazar: Saturday 20 Mareri (2 June) 451 (langlois t2 l.40450-40451). These are modern dates; Lazar's text names the feast of Pentecost (l.40213-40214, rough OCR).

absent_details.note: No held source gives his birth year.

absent_details.detail: Words of his own outside the two histories
absent_details.note: His refusal and his speeches survive only as Elishe and Lazar of Pharp wrote them; no letter or writing of his is held.

claims.claim: At Chalcedon, during the reading of the acts of Constantinople against Eutyches, said "I receive 'the of two;' 'the two' I do not receive" and "I am forced to be impudent, but the matter is one which touches my soul"
claims.witness: Acts of Chalcedon, Session I (npnf214 l.19246-19260)

claims.claim: Succeeded Cyril as bishop of Alexandria
claims.witness: Zachariah, Chronicle (Hamilton-Brooks l.1352-1353: bishop eight years and three months); History of the Patriarchs (Evetts l.34864-34866)

claims.claim: Leo wrote to him in 445 laying down church rules: "you and we ought to be at one in thought and act"
claims.witness: Leo, Letter 9 (npnf212 l.1915-1935); the year is Charles Lett Feltoe's introduction (l.490-494)

claims.claim: Presided at Ephesus in August 449 by the emperor's order
claims.witness: Feltoe's introduction (npnf212 l.636-643); the acts in Perry's English, 'held under the Presidency of Dioscorus' (Perry l.4357)

claims.claim: His sentence on Flavian and Eusebius of Dorylaeum, 'alien from all the Honor of the Priesthood and of the Episcopate'; Flavian answered 'I repudiate you. I protest.'
claims.witness: Acts of Ephesus 449, tr. S. G. F. Perry (l.24090-24137; the quotation runs across a running head at l.24124)

claims.claim: Leo called the council of 449 a meeting 'not of judges but of robbers'
The council's letter to Leo says he 'purposed excommunication' against Leo
claims.witness: Letter 98, from the Council of Chalcedon (npnf212 l.8783-8784); Feltoe dates the excommunication to spring 450 (l.686-688)

claims.claim: Convicted at Chalcedon of suppressing Leo's letter and of procuring the bishops' subscriptions to a blank paper for Flavian's deposition
claims.witness: Evagrius, Ecclesiastical History II.4 (Walford l.3089-3098), summarising the acts; a charge by his opponents

claims.claim: Did not come when summoned three times; told he was deposed on the thirteenth of October
claims.witness: The condemnation sent to Dioscorus (npnf214 l.20072-20092); Feltoe gives Session III, 13 October (npnf212 l.762)

claims.claim: Sentenced to live at Gangra in Paphlagonia
claims.witness: Evagrius II.5 (Walford l.3366-3368); Zachariah III.1-2 (l.2346, 2524-2526); Feltoe (npnf212 l.764-766)

claims.claim: Deposed, by the anti-Chalcedonian account, for saying Christ became incarnate from two natures and not confessing two after the union; refused to sign for his throne: 'Sooner would Dioscorus see his own hand cut off, and the blood falling on the paper, than do such a thing as that'
claims.witness: Zachariah III.1 (Hamilton-Brooks l.2315-2346); partisan. The OCR reads 'two matures' at l.2318, so that phrase is not quoted

claims.claim: Priests, monks and many of the people broke with Proterius and wrote Dioscorus's name in the book of life
In Theopistus's History he tells Pulcheria they may take his throne of wood but not the throne the Messiah prepared for him in heaven
claims.witness: Theopistus, History of Dioscorus, tr. Nau (l.15187-15191); Nau calls these words fine and plausible (l.15206); hagiography

claims.claim: Died in exile at Gangra in 454 (Nau: 4 September)
claims.witness: Feltoe (npnf212 l.765-766); Nau's introduction (Theopistus file l.176-180, 382-384); Evetts's heading gives 444-458 (l.34864)

claims.claim: 'He preserved the orthodox faith, which persists in the see of the evangelist Saint Mark to this day and for ever'; no biography after his banishment was found
claims.witness: History of the Patriarchs, tr. Evetts (l.35104-35110)

contested_claims.claim: Why he was deposed at Chalcedon
contested_claims.sides: The acts and Evagrius: for disregard of the canons, disobedience to the council and refusing three summonses, with charges of suppressing Leo's letter and a blank paper (npnf214 l.20083-20092; Walford l.3089-3098). Zachariah, anti-Chalcedonian: for his teaching of one nature from two, with Anatolius saying 'Not for the faith is Dioscorus deposed' (l.2315-2325).

Nau does not vouch for many details, dates its present form after 512, and reports Assemani's view that it is a fiction (l.420-423, 474-487); Nau also holds that Theopistus did not fabricate every speech (l.424-441).

absent_details.detail: Birth, family and career before he became bishop
absent_details.note: No source used here gives them.
The History of the Patriarchs says no biography after his banishment was found (Evetts l.35104-35107); Theopistus's legend is the only held account of the exile.
None are held as texts of his own; his words come through the acts of 449 and 451 and through his partisans.

claims.claim: Could not begin the book; Euthymius and Sabas appeared to him in sleep; Euthymius put a spoon dipped in a silver flask into his mouth, its look like oil, its taste beyond comparing with honey; on waking he began the work
claims.witness: Cyril of Scythopolis, Life of Euthymius, Latin (l.45569-45591, 45664-45699)

claims.claim: The anchorite Cyriacus told Cyril some of the stories
Born at Melitene, a city of Armenia on the Euphrates, to Paul and Dionysia, childless until a vision promised a son; born in the fourth consulship of Gratian
After his father's death Otreius, bishop of Melitene, made his mother a deaconess and adopted and raised the boy; later ordained priest and given charge of the monasteries
Came to Jerusalem in about his twenty-ninth year; after five years at Pharan left with Theoctistus and found a great cave above a steep torrent

Cyril tells that Aspebetus, a Saracen chief accused before King Yazdegerd for letting Christians flee, went over to the Romans, and that his half-paralysed son Terebon was brought to the cave after a dream and healed
claims.witness: Cyril (l.28522-28545, 28560-28610); Duchesne (l.21176-21194) also has the son healed by Euthymius

claims.claim: Euthymius baptized Aspebetus as Peter and asked Juvenal of Jerusalem for a bishop; Peter was ordained the first bishop of the Camps in Palestine
Chalcedon met in his seventy-fifth year; disciples of his attended; he read the definition and found it right
Theodosius, whom Cyril calls a most destructive deceiver, won over Eudocia and the monks and seized the see of Jerusalem; Euthymius with his monks alone refused his communion
Eudocia, widow of Theodosius II

Eudocia built a tower in the desert, sent Cosmas and Anastasius for him; he told her to accept Chalcedon with the three earlier councils and to hold communion with Juvenal; she did and brought many monks and lay people
Sabas came to him in his eighty-second year and was sent to Theoctistus
Died in the sixteenth year of the emperor Leo, in his ninety-ninth year as the held scan reads, after sixty years in the desert
After Chalcedon, with letters from Marcian, Pulcheria and Leo, Euthymius did his best to calm the monks; his efforts to discipline the solitudes succeeded only in a fairly narrow circle
Cyril calls the Life fit to cheer its readers and rouse them to zeal

contested_claims.claim: Who baptized Aspebetus and made him bishop
contested_claims.sides: Cyril's Latin (l.29083, 30637-30642, 30779): Euthymius baptized him as Peter and asked Juvenal for a bishop for the converts. Louis Duchesne (l.21192-21194): Juvenal baptized him as Peter and consecrated him bishop of the Saracens.

absent_details.note: No writing of Euthymius is held; his teaching reaches us only as Cyril tells it.

absent_details.detail: A readable Greek text and any English translation
absent_details.note: The held file is Cotelier's 1681 Latin in a rough scan; its Greek column cannot be read. The census cites R. M. Price's English (1991), which is not held.

absent_details.detail: Years of birth and death in our reckoning
absent_details.note: Cyril dates by consulship and the emperor's year; the sources used here give no conversion.

claims.claim: After Marcian's death the people and monks of Alexandria seized Timothy and brought him to the great church called Caesarian; two Egyptian bishops were present, and they carried Peter the Iberian on their shoulders to make the third
claims.witness: Zachariah IV.1 (Hamilton-Brooks l.3276-3302), anti-Chalcedonian; Evagrius II.8 (Walford l.3613-3626) names Eusebius of Pelusium and Peter the Iberian, from the Life of Peter

claims.claim: A man of ascetic life, brought from the wilderness by force to Cyril and ordained priest by him; 'of the same faith as Dioscorus'
claims.witness: Zachariah IV.1 (l.3284-3289); Evagrius: formerly a monk, later a presbyter of Alexandria (Walford l.3620-3623)

claims.claim: Called 'the Weasel' in jest by the Proterian party for his thinness
claims.witness: Zachariah IV.1 (l.3305-3307); E. Walford's heading 'THE CAT' (Walford l.3584) and Feltoe 'or the Cat' (npnf212 l.888)

claims.claim: Proterius was killed by Alexandrians 'at the instigation of Timotheus' after fleeing to the baptistery
claims.witness: The petition of the Egyptian bishops and clergy of Alexandria to the emperor Leo, as Evagrius reports and quotes it (Walford l.3640-3664); hostile

claims.claim: A Roman soldier stabbed Proterius
claims.witness: Zachariah IV.2 (l.3380-3392); the Life of Peter the Iberian, as Evagrius reports it (Walford l.3626-3628)

claims.claim: His petition to the emperor Leo: 'I do not agree with the transactions of Chalcedon, because I find in them divisions and cleavage of the dispensation'; the definition of the fathers does not 'require addition'
Dragged from the baptistery font by the clergy of the Proterian party and sent away
Exiled to Gangra, then moved to Cherson
In exile wrote against the Eutychianists as well as the Nestorians
A refutation of Chalcedon and of Leo's Tome by him is held in Armenian
claims.witness: Ter-Mekerttschian and Ter-Minassiantz's edition (file header l.1-9)

claims.claim: Recalled by Basiliscus in the eighteenth year of his banishment
Brought back the bones of Dioscorus in a silver coffin
Zeno gave up expelling him on being told he was old and near death; he died soon after
Chosen after Marcian died in 457; deposed and replaced by 460

contested_claims.sides: The Proterian petition quoted by Evagrius: Alexandrians at Timothy's instigation (Walford l.3640-3664). Zachariah: a Roman soldier (l.3380-3392). The Life of Peter, as Evagrius reports: a soldier (Walford l.3626-3628).
Evagrius and Zachariah: recalled in the eighteenth year (Walford l.5394-5397; l.5219). History of the Patriarchs: banished to Gangra with his brother Anatolius for seven years (Evetts l.35199-35201).

absent_details.detail: Birth, family and the year of his death
absent_details.note: No ancient source used here gives them; Feltoe gives 457 and 460, and Evetts's heading gives his see as 458 to 480.

absent_details.detail: The content of his Armenian refutation
absent_details.note: No translation is held, so it is not quoted or summarised.

claims.claim: Wrote the History at the request of the priest David of the Mamikonian house, in seven chapters, to tell the valiant exploits of the brave and the misery which followed
"Truly, not of our own free will, do we describe, in lamenting tones, all the miseries of which we ourselves have been eye-witnesses"
Birthplace and date unknown
Disciple of Sahak and Mesrop, secretary to Vartan, grandson of Sahak; later bishop of the Amadunians, named in the list of the synod of Artashat in 450
Biographers say he served in Vartan's army in his youth; other writers make him Vartan's secretary; some say he was bishop of the Amadouni and the one in the bishops' list
claims.witness: Langlois, Introduction (langlois t2 l.25717-25733), citing a Venice biography of 1854 and Karékin

claims.claim: The bishops' list names Elishe (Ekhishe/Elisaeus), bishop of the Amadunians, among those assembled at Artashat
Copies the edict of Mihrnerseh, Grand Vizier, and the bishops' answer: "From this belief no one can move us, neither angels nor men—neither fire nor sword, nor water"
In old age withdrew to Ershedunik on Lake Van and died at a very advanced age
Lived as a hermit in a cave on the mountain of Mog, then in a cave by the lake in the Reschdouni country; hardship shortened his life
claims.witness: Langlois, Introduction, after the Venice biography (langlois t2 l.25740-25797)

claims.claim: Some writers place his death in 480
Resisted Greek influence on the language more than any of his fellow students; the Armenians rightly count the History among the most brilliant pieces of their classical literature
Wrote a Discourse to the Solitaries and commentaries on Joshua and Judges
A Nestorian named Barsouma borrowed the History and struck out the mentions of the Ardzruni house; Elishe died before revising it
claims.witness: Langlois, reporting Thomas Ardsruni (langlois t2 l.25945-25989)

claims.claim: "Concord is the mother of good; and Dissension, the nurse of evil"

contested_claims.sides: Neumann, citing Thomas Ardsruni (l.595-600): retired to Ershedunik on Lake Van and died at a very advanced age. Langlois, after the Venice biography (langlois t2 l.25740-25797): a hermit in two caves, his life shortened by hardships. Langlois's note: some writers give 480 (l.25816-25817).

contested_claims.claim: The supplement on the sufferings of the priests
contested_claims.sides: Neumann (l.738-748): a separate work the editors joined to the History. Langlois (langlois t2 l.25910-25925): Elishe's own, against critics who give it to an anonymous continuator.

absent_details.detail: A modern debate on the date of the History
absent_details.note: The Library's file note on Neumann's translation says the History's dating is discussed in scholarship; no held work sets out a later date. Neumann and Langlois both treat him as a fifth-century writer.
Langlois says his birthplace and date are unknown; Neumann's 'grandson of Sahag the Great' refers to Vartan, not to Elishe.
Named by Langlois and Neumann; not in the held translations.

claims.claim: Felix, bishop of Abbir for forty-four years, paralysed and unable to feel or speak, was among those exiled; Victor and others asked that he stay at Carthage; the king, as reported, said wild oxen should drag him; they carried him tied across a mule like a log
claims.witness: Victor, History II.26-27 (Petschenig l.2854-2863; Halm l.1772-1776, 'quadraginta quattuor')

claims.claim: The manuscripts title him bishop of the patria Vitensis
Pampinianus, venerable bishop of 'our city', was burned with red-hot iron plates; 'our city' is Vita
claims.witness: Victor I (Petschenig l.1241-1242); Halm's note (Halm l.604)

claims.claim: Writes in the sixtieth year since the Vandals, a cruel and savage people, crossed the strait from Spain to Africa
Calls their faith the Arian heresy

4,966 bishops, priests, deacons and other church members were sent to exile in the desert; gathered at Sicca and Lares they cried that they were Christians and Catholics; Victor and others could go in, encourage them and celebrate the mysteries
Copies Huneric's edict, dated at Carthage six days before the Kalends of March; Petschenig's margin gives 484
Victor likely inserted the Book of Faith into his history himself

At Tipasa in Mauretania the king had the tongues and right hands of those who refused the Arian bishop cut off, and they spoke as before; the subdeacon Reparatus could be found at Constantinople, honoured at the palace of Zeno
Honoric cut out the tongues of many, who up to Procopius's time went about in Byzantium speaking
claims.witness: Procopius of Caesarea, Wars III.8 (l.913-919), an outside witness

claims.claim: Calls on the angels of God to see Africa, once upheld by so many churches, now sitting a widow and cast down
The prologue is printed in brackets and discussed beside the spurious additions as very obscure

contested_claims.claim: That the Tipasa confessors spoke after their tongues were cut out
contested_claims.sides: Victor (Petschenig l.5953-5961) tells it as a wonder and names Reparatus at Constantinople; Procopius of Caesarea (l.913-919) says such people still spoke in Byzantium in his day, two of them losing speech later. No held source denies it; both witnesses report it, and the brief tells it as their report.

absent_details.detail: His birth, family, career and death
absent_details.note: No source used here gives them; his life is known only from what his History says.
Only the rough 1605 English OCR is held; John Moorhead's English (1992) is in copyright and not held.

claims.claim: Hurried home from Byzantium hoping to dance at weddings; found himself at a grave, weeping; did not arrive in time to close Sahak's and Mesrop's eyes or hear their last words
claims.witness: Moses of Khoren, History III.68, the lament (Langlois t.2 l.25495-25503)

claims.claim: The lament is the last chapter of the History as held; three books, from the first ancestors to the deaths of Sahak and Mesrop
claims.witness: Table of book III (Langlois t.2 l.19907-19913); book I opens on the genealogy of Greater Armenia (l.8715-8721)

claims.claim: Wrote at the request of Sahak Bagratuni
claims.witness: Moses, History I.1 (Langlois t.2 l.8723-8731; table l.8586)

claims.claim: His patron was the Bagratid prince proclaimed marzban in 481 by Armenians in revolt against Persia

Sahak and Mesrop sent him to Alexandria to study; passed through Edessa and its archives, the holy places of Palestine; at Alexandria a new Plato whose pupil he was not found worthy to be; winds drove him to Italy; a short stay at Athens; then towards Byzantium
The new Plato is Cyril of Alexandria
claims.witness: Langlois's note, 'sans doute' (l.24853-24854); the Mekhitarist preface, 'forse' (ita l.136-138)

claims.claim: Lived ten years apart and poor; made bishop of Bagrevand by the patriarch Kiud after Eznik of Kolb died
claims.witness: Langlois, Introduction (l.7852-7869), citing Saint-Martin; Langlois adds that tradition has surrounded his life with details history has not kept (l.7870-7874)

claims.claim: Lived past a hundred, into Zeno's reign
claims.witness: Thomas Artsruni, as cited in Langlois's Introduction and note 4 (l.7876-7881, 7896-7897); Langlois says his age cannot be fixed exactly

claims.claim: Born in the second half of the fourth century, at Khorni in Daron
claims.witness: Langlois, Introduction (l.7787-7790); the Mekhitarist preface gives the township of Corene in Daron (ita l.122)

claims.claim: Almost nothing precise is known of Moses of Khoren
claims.witness: Frédéric Macler, introduction to Stephen of Taron (macler1917 l.671-674)

claims.claim: The History earned him his place at the head of the historians of his nation
The rhetorical treatises attributed to him may be by another Moses of the eighth century
Some critics deny him the Geography; the Book of Chreiai has been thought apocryphal; Langlois defends both

contested_claims.sides: Fifth century: Langlois, Introduction (born in the later fourth century, l.7787-7790; patron's revolt of 481, l.7963-7965) and the Mekhitarist preface (ita l.122-165), both drawing his life from the History. A later date: argued by no work held in the Library; the Library file header of the Italian edition (l.4-5) and the era 3 scan note only that modern scholarship debates it. Macler (l.671-674): almost nothing precise is known of him.

absent_details.detail: A held work arguing a later date for the History
absent_details.note: Harnack's bibliography lists Carrière's 1895 study of the Abgar legend in Moses (harnack chronologie l.9336-9337) by title only; the study is not held.

absent_details.detail: Birth and death years, and any source for his life outside his own History
absent_details.note: Langlois and the Mekhitarists draw on the History and later Armenian tradition (Thomas Artsruni, Saint-Martin); no contemporary witness is held.

absent_details.detail: An Armenian text or an English translation of the History
absent_details.note: Only the French of Langlois's collection and the Mekhitarist Italian of 1850 are held.

claims.claim: Confessed to Acacius that Satan stirred up a quarrel between him and Babai; gave way to bishops Babai meant to judge; held the synod of Beth Lapat and made canons by human passion; called it contrary to Christianity; had twice written to annul it
claims.witness: His third letter, Synodicon orientale (Chabot l.35391-35406, 35454-35463)

claims.claim: The synod of Beth Lapat in April 484; the reconciliation at Beth Edrai in August 485; the letters between September 485 and February 486
claims.witness: Chabot's notes (l.20239, 35228, 35643-35656), from the first letter's own dating, the month Ab of the second year of King Balash (l.35210)

claims.claim: First a slave of Mare of Qardu; studied at the school of Edessa, still there in 449; expelled at Ibas's death in 457; bishop through King Peroz
claims.witness: Chabot's note (l.20229-20235); Simeon of Beth Arsham as cited by Abbeloos and Lamy (Bar Hebraeus vol. III l.3651-3657, 3676-3683)

claims.claim: Consecrated bishop in 435
claims.witness: Elias and Ebedjesu of Nisibis, as cited by Addai Scher (Barhadbeshabba, Cause, l.20624-20625, 20820); a Vatican manuscript cited by Abbeloos and Lamy (l.3651-3653)

claims.claim: Drought for two years; tribes subject to Persia raided Roman lands; he brought a Roman general to Nisibis to meet the marzban; raiders struck while they feasted; the Romans blamed him, so he could not go to the catholicos
Nisibis troubled and tossed like a stormy sea; feared the king would issue an edict against all Christians
Accused Babai to Peroz as a Roman spy, and Peroz had Babai killed
claims.witness: Bar Hebraeus (vol. III l.3836-3847), hostile; Mari ibn Sulayman (Gismondi l.14355-14364), who adds that Barsauma soon regretted it; Chabot after 'Amr (l.20206-20208)

claims.claim: Led Persian soldiers against those who refused his teaching; a report of 7,700 dead
claims.witness: Bar Hebraeus (vol. III l.3956-3960, 4052-4075), hostile; Chabot calls him very inaccurate on Barsauma (Chabot l.41054-41056)

claims.claim: Married a nun and made marriage lawful for bishops and priests
claims.witness: Mari ibn Sulayman (l.14386-14387); Bar Hebraeus calls her a concubine (vol. III l.3758-3764)

claims.claim: Quick mind; wrote many homilies; welcomed Narsai to Nisibis and helped him found the school
Death year unknown, after 491; killed by nuns of Tur Abdin with the keys of their cells, or buried in the church of Mar Jacob at Nisibis
claims.witness: Chabot (l.20206-20212, 35643-35647); Bar Hebraeus's two reports (vol. III l.4546-4552)

contested_claims.claim: When he became bishop of Nisibis
contested_claims.sides: After his expulsion from Edessa in 457: Chabot (l.20229-20235); Simeon of Beth Arsham, as Abbeloos and Lamy cite him (vol. III l.3654-3657). In 435: Elias and Ebedjesu of Nisibis, as Addai Scher cites them (PO 4 l.20624-20625, 20820); a Vatican manuscript, as Abbeloos and Lamy note (l.3651-3653).
Yes: Bar Hebraeus (l.3836-3847), hostile; Mari ibn Sulayman (l.14355-14364), with his regret; 'Amr, as Chabot reports (l.20206-20208). His own letters speak only of a quarrel (l.35397-35398).
Mari: a nun he married, making marriage lawful for clergy (l.14386-14387). Bar Hebraeus: a woman kept in his cell whom he called his lawful wife (l.3758-3764).

absent_details.note: Chabot's note gives only that he was first a slave of Mare of Qardu; no held line gives his birth or parents.
Chabot says the date is unknown, after 491; Bar Hebraeus gives two reports and settles neither.
The compiler of the Synodicon left the synod out; Chabot gathers fragments (l.41049-41052), which this profile does not use.

claims.claim: Warned by a friend that he would be thrown into the fire unless he fled that night; asked Persians at the church to carry his books, all his treasure, to Nisibis
claims.witness: Barhadbeshabba, History, ch. XXXI (PO 9 l.36830-36839), a saint's life

claims.claim: The history written near the end of the sixth century; its author probably the bishop of Halwan of 605
From the land of Ma'alta, village of 'Ain Dulba; went to school at seven and learned the Psalter in nine months
Led the school of Edessa twenty years
claims.witness: Barhadbeshabba, History (PO 9 l.36626-36634) and Cause (PO 4 l.20553-20559); Connolly (l.279-280, 316-317)

claims.claim: Accused at Edessa of following Theodore and Nestorius, of siding with Persia and of wishing to betray the city
Left Edessa in 457
Barsauma persuaded him to stay at Nisibis and bought a camel stable near the church for the school; students came from all sides
"Edessa was darkened, but Nisibis shone forth"
claims.witness: Barhadbeshabba in Connolly's English (l.4494, note citing Mingana)

claims.claim: With the school of Nisibis began the formation of what is now known as the Nestorian Church
Barsauma's wife grew jealous of the crowds at his door; he withdrew to Kefar Mari and wrote a poem on her; read at Nisibis, the bishop repented and recalled him
claims.witness: Barhadbeshabba, History (PO 9 l.37118-37175, 37210-37215); later Mari (Gismondi l.14104-14108, 14268-14271) and Bar Hebraeus (vol. III l.4410-4420)

claims.claim: All his skill in Scripture came from Theodore's commentaries, by his homily on the three Doctors
Answered Jacob of Sarug's verse with a verse homily for each day of the year, in twelve volumes
Called Narsai the leper
claims.witness: Simeon of Beth Arsham, quoted from Assemani by Abbeloos and Lamy (Bar Hebraeus vol. III l.3690, 3787-3788); hostile

claims.claim: Buried in a good old age; death in 502 or in 503 or 504
claims.witness: Barhadbeshabba (PO 9 l.37410-37412); Connolly after Mingana (l.297-302); Nau (l.37421-37428)

claims.claim: "instead of our clay He has made us spiritual gold"
claims.witness: Homily XXII (B), On Baptism, tr. Connolly (l.6855-6856)

contested_claims.sides: 457: Connolly after Mingana (l.257-260, 299-301). After 471: Barhadbeshabba's naming of the bishop, if it stands, as Nau notes (PO 9 l.36699-36705); Nau himself prefers an earlier bishop, Nonnus, which keeps 457 to 471.

contested_claims.claim: His years at Nisibis and his death
contested_claims.sides: Forty years plus six at the monastery: Barhadbeshabba, History (PO 9 l.37410-37411). Forty-five: Barhadbeshabba, Cause (PO 4 l.20746), giving 502 for Connolly after Mingana (l.297-302). Fifty: Bar Hebraeus (vol. III l.4554-4557), giving 507, as Nau reports (PO 9 l.37425-37427). Nau: 503 or 504 (l.37427-37428).

contested_claims.claim: The cause of the break with Barsauma
contested_claims.sides: Barhadbeshabba: the jealousy of Barsauma's wife (PO 9 l.37123-37166). Mari: the same woman's envy (l.14268-14271). Bar Hebraeus, hostile: a quarrel over a concubine, and Barsauma expelled him (l.4410-4413).

contested_claims.claim: Whether the Exposition of the Mysteries (Homily XVII) is his
contested_claims.sides: One or two late authorities: a writer of the thirteenth century (Connolly l.170-172). Connolly: genuine (l.2412-2416).

absent_details.note: No held source gives it. Nau reckons from Barhadbeshabba's numbers that he lived from about 400 (with a query) to 503 or 504 (PO 9 l.37427-37428); the Library header's c. 413 is not used.
Connolly reports 360 credited by Ebedjesu and 47 printed by Mingana (l.261-263); the Library holds four in English.
